reason: The core fact is confirmed. caniuse.com/webxr (opened) lists Safari on iOS as "Not supported" for every version, including 27.0 and the 27.1-27.2 range, with no entry beyond 27.2; desktop Safari is "Disabled by default" from 13 through 27.1/Technology Preview; Chrome for Android (154) and Samsung Internet are "Partial support". Independent sources agree: MDN browser-compat-data (api/Navigator.json, "xr" entry) gives safari_ios version_added=false (chrome 79, samsunginternet_android 11.2), and WebKit's own posts say WebXR shipped only on visionOS (behind a flag in visionOS 1.1/Safari 17.4, immersive-vr on visionOS 2/Safari 18) with no mention of iOS or iPadOS. Apple's AR Quick Look page confirms Quick Look on iPhone/iPad requires iOS 12 or later and uses USDZ (and .reality) files launched from Safari. Two parts of the claim are overstated rather than wrong: (1) "any in-browser AR overlay is Android-only" is true only for WebXR-based AR; non-WebXR WebAR that uses getUserMedia plus WebGL (for example AR.js, whose docs say it "works on every phone with webgl and webrtc" and whose LocAR.js fork lists iOS Safari fixes) runs in iOS Safari, and Variant Launch delivers WebXR-style AR on iPhone from a Safari link via an App Clip; (2) "must go through AR Quick Look with a USDZ file" should read "the only system-native route is AR Quick Look, which accepts USDZ or .reality files". Note: the WebSearch budget was exhausted this turn, so verification used WebFetch on known URLs only.
corrected_claim: Safari on iOS has no WebXR Device API support in any version listed by caniuse, up to and including 27.2 (https://caniuse.com/webxr; MDN compat data likewise records safari_ios: false, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mdn/browser-compat-data/main/api/Navigator.json). Apple ships WebXR only on visionOS (https://webkit.org/blog/15443/news-from-wwdc24-webkit-in-safari-18-beta/), and desktop Safari has it disabled by default. WebXR-based in-browser AR is therefore Android-only on mobile (Chrome for Android and Samsung Internet, partial support). On iPhone, the system-native route is Apple AR Quick Look, launched from Safari with a USDZ or .reality file and requiring iOS 12 or later (https://developer.apple.com/augmented-reality/quick-look/). Non-WebXR WebAR libraries that use camera access and WebGL (for example AR.js, https://ar-js-org.github.io/AR.js-Docs/) still run in iOS Safari, and services such as Variant Launch (https://launch.variant3d.com/) bridge WebXR content to iPhone through an App Clip.
